video_title: How AI Becomes a Political Crisis | Anton Leicht - Carnegie Fellow
gist: Carnegie fellow Anton Leicht and host Jordan Schneider map the domestic political economy of AI in the US: they expect the midterms to stay quiet on AI but the 2027 Congress to legislate, argue that a 0.5–1% unemployment uptick or one hard-hit profession is enough to make AI a front-page campaign issue, and work through the policy toolkit — junior-hiring subsidies, corporate income tax versus a 'token tax', sovereign AI stakes, professional carve-outs. They argue a true development pause is structurally impossible because no politician will crash the data-center capex rally, that live 'pauses' are really data-center construction moratoriums, that a frontier-development slowdown would be an asymmetric treaty handing China time to indigenize its semiconductor supply chain, and that classifier-based safety and open weights are on an unresolvable collision course.

insights.claim: Anton Leicht expects the 2026 US midterms to stay relatively quiet on AI because politicians don't yet know which way the wind blows or what the specific policy asks are, with the real legislative window opening in the 2027 Congress once post-midterm polling shows how salient the issue was.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Gives a roughly 12–18 month runway before AI-specific federal legislation becomes a live risk to AI-exposed equities; policy risk is a 2027 story, not a 2026 one.
insights.quote: I think then we'll probably be in a window where like actual policy that actually gets like sort of some some amount of national attention actually happens

insights.claim: Three or four separate AI trends — government waking up to cyber implications, populist flanks on both sides hunting for visible symbols before the midterms, and fast real-world adoption — are compounding simultaneously, and it is still unclear whether they fuse into one 'AI is big' political story or die as three separate ones.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Watch for narrative convergence: three separate stories are absorbable, one fused story is what produces binding legislation and a sector de-rating.

insights.claim: It will not take 10% unemployment to make AI politically explosive — a half-percent to one-percent move, or a single industry or geography getting hit fast, is enough, because the US is coming off a long stretch of essentially no unemployment and any increase is a shock to the system.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: The political trigger level for AI backlash is far below the macro level that would matter for earnings — headline risk arrives long before the fundamentals do.
insights.quote: it's not going to take 10% unemployment to freak people out. It will take like a half a percent or 1%

insights.claim: Leicht sees essentially no path where AI employment does not become a big salient issue, because the political narrative components are already loaded: tech oligarchs building huge data centers, coastal elites versus the rest of the country, and tech CEOs aligning with the administration.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Assume political salience as a base case, not a tail risk, when modeling permitting, siting and taxation for AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: Firms are already blaming layoffs on AI that are not substantively about AI because it makes a convenient story, and Leicht expects more of that plus junior hiring freezes as firms experiment with agents — meaning the political narrative will run ahead of the measured displacement.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Treat 'AI layoffs' headlines as an unreliable proxy for actual automation; the attribution is strategically useful to management and to politicians alike.
insights.quote: We'll see junior hiring freezes in some domains because people will start experimenting with using agents instead.

insights.claim: Displaced junior white-collar workers are a far more explosive political story than displaced 55-year-old steelworkers because the 'study hard, work hard, get an ambitious white-collar job' pipeline is an American-dream channel that far more voters empathize with.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Youth/graduate unemployment prints are the highest-beta political indicator for AI regulation risk — watch them over aggregate unemployment.
insights.quote: there is a sort of like American dream characteristic to this idea

insights.claim: Opposition to data centers has already mobilized around abstract and partly fictitious concerns such as water usage, showing that latent hostility rather than acute harm is driving the backlash.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: Siting and permitting risk for data-center buildouts is driven by sentiment, not by verifiable local impact — mitigation spending may not buy political cover.
insights.quote: the whole water thing

insights.claim: The most important data on how AI is affecting labor — usage, diffusion, and the split between augmentative and automation-heavy workloads — sits inside the AI labs, not with government statistical agencies.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Lab-published usage data is currently the only real-time read on AI displacement; investors get an information edge from it before official statistics move.
insights.quote: a lot of the most important and most interesting data is inside the labs

insights.claim: Anthropic's economic index is cited as the type of usable diffusion data that exists, but it is one lab's data, is not standardized against other labs, and may skew because of that lab's specific consumer base.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Don't extrapolate one lab's usage mix to the whole economy; cross-lab aggregation, if it ever happens, would be a genuinely new macro dataset.

insights.claim: The correct policy response inverts entirely depending on whether current AI workloads are augmentative or automating: if augmentative, governments should hasten adoption to build a resilient workforce, but if adoption is already producing outright displacement, there is a case to slow it down.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The augmentation-versus-automation ratio is the single variable that determines whether governments become AI accelerants or brakes — a key swing factor for adoption-driven revenue.

insights.claim: BLS and productivity data are too slow, too spotty and too coarsely tuned to detect AI-driven labor displacement in time to inform policy, so policymakers will be acting on anecdote and media coverage rather than statistics.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: Expect policy to be triggered by vivid single-firm events rather than data releases — a source of abrupt, hard-to-forecast regulatory moves.

insights.claim: Leicht identifies an economy-wide coordination failure in which every firm has a short-term incentive to skip junior hiring and use agents instead, and the result is that a whole cohort never matures into the five-to-eight-year experienced workers needed to orchestrate AI agents later.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: If real, firms that keep hiring juniors through the transition own a scarce mid-level orchestration layer in five years — a quiet differentiator in services businesses.
insights.quote: we suddenly lose out on educating and building out this entire generation of of junior white collar workers

insights.claim: The compensation playbook used for past technological displacement — wage insurance and early retirement for 55-year-old steelworkers — cannot be applied to AI displacement because the losers are young workers at the start of a career, not workers near the end of one.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Existing adjustment-assistance machinery is unusable here, so any political response will require new and less predictable policy instruments.

insights.claim: Leicht's tentative preferred intervention is a targeted subsidy or tax-code change making 22-to-27-year-old workers cheaper to hire, which he describes as the least bad option rather than a good one.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A junior-hiring subsidy is the most likely first concrete AI-labor policy — a mild tailwind for labor-intensive services employers if it arrives.
insights.quote: it is tentatively the least bad version of fixing this problem that we might be able to come up with

insights.claim: Leicht flags that any wage guarantee or jobs subsidy risks brute-force subsidizing an economic structure that works at one level of technological deployment and breaks at the next, calcifying the labor market rather than letting it transition.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Subsidy design determines whether AI-era labor policy is a temporary bridge or a permanent drag on reallocation — a long-horizon productivity variable.

insights.claim: Leicht concedes the junior subsidy could be a bridge to nowhere — once it lapses, workers may simply not be hired and layoffs creep up the experience ladder — but argues that in that world a subsidy system doubles as pre-built infrastructure for jobs-guarantee-style redistribution.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Frames employment subsidies as the on-ramp to eventual redistribution, implying a structurally higher long-run corporate tax burden rather than a UBI financed some other way.

insights.claim: Leicht doubts that the plumber, nurse, schoolteacher, data-center-electrician transition can quantitatively absorb displaced white-collar workers, since at some point the data centers and infrastructure are built.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the consensus 'everyone retrains into the trades' answer, and implies data-center construction employment is itself a temporary absorber.
insights.quote: I'm not so sure how many jobs the sort of plumber, nurse, school teacher, data center, electrician transition can really absorb in the long run

insights.claim: Leicht argues that elite performance in narrow competitive environments like professional esports or chess transfers poorly to complex careers, because processing speed and drilled execution are rarely the bottleneck, while more strategic and team-based games transfer somewhat better.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A caution against assuming that any high-intensity skill environment produces transferable human capital — relevant to retraining bets and to talent screening.
insights.quote: that is not really something that translates in any way

insights.claim: Leicht's fiscal argument is that if AI erodes labor tax revenue while simultaneously creating the need to fund subsidies, jobs guarantees or retraining, the revenue must be replaced — and corporate income tax is the least bad instrument because it is agnostic about whether the money ends up with model developers, chip designers or adopters.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A higher corporate income tax is the most probable AI-era revenue mechanism — a broad, non-sector-specific headwind to after-tax margins rather than a targeted hit on AI names.

insights.claim: Leicht points to the G20 global minimum corporate tax floor as precedent that an international version of AI-era corporate taxation is not absurd, noting it got pretty far along even though it did not ultimately happen.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Cross-border tax coordination could resurface with AI as the forcing function, limiting the durability of jurisdictional tax arbitrage.
insights.quote: the G20 sort of minimum floor thing didn't actually happen, but it was pretty far along

insights.claim: A 'token tax' on AI usage is badly designed because it hits the most ambitious adopters hardest and the least-adopting legacy firms least — the opposite of what a policymaker worried about labor disruption should want.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: If a token tax gains traction, the losers are AI-forward enterprise adopters and the inference-consumption layer, not the laggards a populist would intend to protect.
insights.quote: it hits it hits the like ambitious adopters the hardest and it hits the sort of legacy firms that do the least adopting the least

insights.claim: Leicht generalizes the token-tax flaw into a rule: any AI-specific tax also specifically hits the augmentative uses of AI that would most help avoid the worst labor-market outcomes.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for screening proposed AI taxes: if it cannot distinguish augmentation from substitution, it is self-defeating and likely to be abandoned or watered down.
insights.quote: whenever you try to specifically hit AI it turns out you also specifically hit augmentative uses of AI

insights.claim: The tax code currently favors capex on AI buildout and possibly agent spend far more than it favors hiring humans and paying payroll tax, an asymmetry Leicht argues should be evened out so it is not irrational to hire a human for work a million tokens could do.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Tax-code asymmetry is a real and underdiscussed accelerant of substitution; equalizing it would directly change the build-versus-hire calculus at the enterprise level.
insights.quote: the capex on like AI buildout and maybe even on agent spend is just so much more favored by the tax code than you know hiring humans

insights.claim: Taking government equity stakes specifically in AI developers creates a regulatory capture problem, because state revenue then depends on that narrow subset of the economy doing well and policy gets steered to make value accrue at the developer layer rather than at the infrastructure or adopter layer.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: If the state takes AI-lab equity, expect policy tilted to protect lab margins at the expense of infrastructure providers, startups and adopters — a relative-value distortion across the AI stack.
insights.quote: you just have the sort of regulatory capture problem

insights.claim: Leicht argues a broad, diversified government AI stake is self-defeating: most adopters and startups are unlisted and cannot be bought, and if you diversify enough across chip designers, labs, pharma and manufacturing beneficiaries you have simply recreated the stock market and called it an AI stake.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Any credible sovereign AI-value-capture scheme collapses into broad equity ownership, which argues for broad-market exposure over a narrow AI basket as the policy-hedged position.
insights.quote: So at some point you've just recreated the stock market from first principles

insights.claim: Leicht says it is already odd for a president to be indexed to the stock market, but worse to be indexed to a narrow basket of roughly four companies in one sector via a government account scheme.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Concentrated state ownership would tie policy support explicitly to a handful of names, raising both their political protection and their political-risk beta.
insights.quote: but I would prefer them to be indexed on how the stock market did relative to this little Trump account thing

insights.claim: Leicht predicts a race to the bottom in which many professions lobby for arbitrary human-in-the-loop laws — accounting must be done by a human, legal tasks must be done by a human — as the main defensive response to automation.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Licensed-profession lobbying is the near-term regulatory battleground; incumbents in accounting and legal services get a temporary earnings shield.
insights.quote: I think we'll see almost the race to the bottom on this

insights.claim: Leicht argues professional carve-outs are unsustainable because vertically integrated AI-native competitors offering 'not quite legal advice' will emerge, and enforcing a ban would require stopping the models from answering, then stopping clever prompts, then stopping open-weight models.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Regulatory moats around licensed services are a delay, not a defense — a case for shorting the durability of incumbent services multiples rather than the services themselves.

insights.claim: Protected legacy firms will survive on risk-averse customers for a while, but Leicht expects efficiency gains so large that the next-best outside service simply eats their lunch on price.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The margin compression in protected services arrives through price competition from adjacent, differently-structured providers rather than through direct displacement.
insights.quote: the efficiency increases are just going to be so brutal that you know the the next best like outside service just just eats their lunch

insights.claim: Leicht uses Germany as the cautionary case: extremely strong labor protections raised the bar to hiring, deterred speculative new firms, and left an economy whose most valuable firms are nearly 100 years old and which struggles to reallocate talent toward EVs or defense production.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The failure mode to price is calcification: protections that look stabilizing in a slow-technology economy destroy competitiveness when the technology frontier moves.
insights.quote: There's not there's not a lot of new dynamic new entrance.

themes.theme: Pause politics and the capex cycle

insights.claim: Leicht's central reason a genuine AI development pause will not happen is political rather than technical: no one is going to pass policy that crashes the stock market on their watch and sends the data-center infrastructure rally to hell.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The size of the AI capex rally is itself the strongest structural protection against restrictive AI policy — market cap has become a policy constraint.
insights.quote: no one is going to pass policy on that that crashes the stock market on their watch that makes this infrastructure rally go to hell

insights.claim: Leicht argues 10% unemployment would produce a pause on AI deployment, not on AI development, because the public reaction would be that the systems are suddenly everywhere rather than that they are getting too capable too fast.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The regulatory tail risk sits on commercial deployment and agent rollout — i.e. on revenue — not on training compute, which is the opposite of what most safety-framed risk models assume.
insights.quote: I think a pause on AI deployment definitely follows from 10% from 10% unemployment

insights.claim: A deployment pause would push labs to deploy inference internally and keep building better models quietly, so the underlying risks continue to emerge in a different and less visible shape.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Restricting external deployment redirects capability gains inside labs, concentrating rather than reducing capability — and shifting value away from external API revenue.

insights.claim: The pauses actually being discussed at the policy level are not pauses on AI development but moratoriums on data-center construction, and Leicht thinks a broad populist base plus some moderates can be rallied behind exactly that.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The live, politically achievable restriction is on physical buildout — the direct exposure is to power, land, construction and siting timelines, not to model training.
insights.quote: their pauses on data center construction specifically

insights.claim: Leicht argues the broad anti-AI coalition cannot hold because its members want incompatible pauses: people worried about labor impacts are happy pushing development into internal deployment, which is precisely what hardcore safety advocates would object to.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Coalition incoherence is the main reason to discount headline counts of 'anti-AI' sentiment when forecasting whether restrictive legislation actually passes.

insights.claim: Leicht frames a narrow pause on frontier development as effectively an asymmetric treaty, because frontier AI is one of the few things the US does far better than China, so a pause disproportionately gives up the American edge.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Any US-only slowdown proposal faces a national-security veto that makes it very unlikely to survive contact with policymakers.

insights.claim: Leicht's strongest objection to a multi-year pause is that it hands China time to indigenize its semiconductor supply chain — possibly reaching domestic DUV and eventually frontier chips at scale — so the race restarts at a point where the US no longer has a chip edge, which he calls strategically almost fatal.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The chip-supply-chain lead is a depreciating asset with a clock on it; policy that buys time is, in this framing, spending the core US strategic advantage.
insights.quote: then you just restart the race at a later point where you no longer have the chip edge and that just seems like strategically almost fatal

insights.claim: For a slowdown treaty to work it would need to verify and constrain Chinese industrial policy and indigenization, not just training runs — a verification problem Leicht dismisses as crazy, leaving only parallel domestic safety work of the kind Matt Sheehan describes in 'AI safety in parallel'.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A US-China grand bargain on AI is not investable; best case is information-sharing on safety practices, which does not slow capex or capability.

insights.claim: Jordan Schneider notes that a pause imposed for labor-market reasons would never be unpaused, unlike a safety-motivated pause with a defined threshold.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: Labor-driven deployment restrictions should be modeled as permanent regime change rather than as a temporary drag on adoption curves.

insights.claim: The administration's current comfort with frontier models rests on guardrails and classifiers — refusing dangerous requests or rerouting prompts to a weaker model — and Leicht says that is why they were ultimately satisfied with releasing the model referred to as fable.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Classifier quality is the de facto regulatory gate for frontier releases, making safety tooling a licence-to-operate cost rather than an optional investment.

insights.claim: The classifier-based safety approach fundamentally does not work with open weights because the guards can be trained out, so the premise that a model can be capable yet refuse dangerous requests collapses the moment weights are released.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Governments that regulate via classifiers must eventually restrict open-weight releases — a direct threat to open-model strategies and the ecosystems built on them.
insights.quote: the classifier based approach just doesn't work with open source

insights.claim: The open-source defense-favored argument — release capabilities to attackers and defenders alike and trust defenders to move faster — works decently for cyber but has no obvious analog for biorisk, since nobody can stockpile vaccines for pathogens a model has not designed yet.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The open-source policy case is risk-domain-specific; a single biosecurity incident would remove its intellectual foundation almost overnight.

insights.claim: Leicht sees an unresolvable collision course between national-security policymakers who structurally want to control dangerous technology and open source, which is inherently uncontrollable and distributed.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Open-weight availability at the frontier should be treated as time-limited by policy, not as a permanent feature of the AI landscape.

insights.claim: Leicht says the only intellectually honest resolutions are either closing weights or accepting that widely available powerful open models end the nation state as it has existed, and that the position claiming the two trains simply pass each other is the dishonest version.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A useful test for open-source advocacy: proponents who deny the tension are unlikely to survive the first serious incident with their policy position intact.
insights.quote: That's just the dishonest version of dealing with this

insights.claim: Leicht reads Nvidia's pro-open-source letter as very cleverly timed — it lands while closed models are already above dangerous thresholds but open models are not, and while the salient risk vector is cyber, the one domain where the open-source story is most defensible — but he doubts it will age well.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Nvidia's open-weights advocacy is a timing trade on a policy window that is expected to close, implying eventual reversal risk to open-ecosystem demand assumptions.
insights.quote: So like as always very clever by Nvidia, but I'm not sure it's going to age particularly well.

insights.claim: Jordan Schneider argues open models have not yet crossed the threshold of doing real damage but inevitably will, with the only plausible exception being that models get closed because China itself gets spooked about proliferation.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: Chinese policy on open-weight releases is an underwatched swing factor for the entire global open-model ecosystem.
insights.quote: we still haven't hit the open source threshold of these models actually being able to do real damage

themes.theme: How AI policy actually gets made

insights.claim: Jordan Schneider argues the episode in which an administration explicitly and publicly committed to doing nothing about AI suddenly imposed intrusive and dramatic measures proves that political priors explain only twenty or thirty percent of AI policy outcomes.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: Stated policy positions are weak predictors of AI regulation; scenario-weight a sudden reversal triggered by a single capability event.

insights.claim: The current US AI governance framework built around the executive order is dramatically overindexed on cyber as a threat model, purely because the incidental triggering event involved a model's cyber capabilities.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Compliance regimes are being built around a cyber template, leaving a structural gap that a non-cyber incident would expose and force a second, more disruptive policy round.
insights.quote: dramatically overindexed on cyber as a threat model specifically

insights.claim: The cyber-derived governance template — give defenders lead-time access, patch the holes, then release the model more broadly — does not generalize to biorisk, where there is no equivalent hardening step short of stockpiling vaccines for pathogens that do not exist yet.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Expect the pre-deployment-access model to break publicly the first time a biocapability evaluation triggers it, prompting far blunter restrictions.

insights.claim: Leicht attributes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's heavy involvement in AI policy conversations to the incidental fact that banks got spooked about cyber risk and reached out to Treasury, illustrating that which agency owns AI policy is a matter of happenstance.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Treasury rather than a tech-focused agency is currently a key node in AI policy, which matters for who gets lobbied and which regulatory instruments get used.
insights.quote: a lot of banks specifically got freaked out about the cyber risk and they reach out to Treasury

insights.claim: Leicht's structural explanation for policy overreaction is capacity: because no expertise, awareness or minimal-intervention machinery was built in advance, the first real breakthrough necessarily produced a maximal response.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Absence of regulatory infrastructure raises rather than lowers policy tail risk — quiet periods should be read as building overreaction potential, not as safety.
insights.quote: you just like close your eyes to something that is like like slowly happening and starting to happen more and more for long enough then at some point you will overreact

insights.claim: Leicht, a veteran of German politics, says the US policy environment is dramatically more permeable to outside ideas than Europe's, partly because legacy sources of ideas are not up to speed on AI, while European political culture is much more risk-averse and prefers ideas laundered through established channels.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: New AI policy ideas reach US decision-makers first and fastest, so US policy is both the leading indicator and the more volatile jurisdiction to track.
insights.quote: the permeability just like ideas and things you put out there is just so much higher

insights.claim: Leicht says the rest of the world's AI conversation runs at a substantial lag to the US — with awareness only shifting after the fable release — and calls that lag its own geopolitical problem.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Non-US AI regulation should be modeled as a delayed echo of US developments, giving a forecastable lead time on European policy shifts.
insights.quote: always add like a substantial lag compared to the US conversation which is its own geopolitical problem

insights.claim: Leicht argues AI policy decisions tend to emerge without an identifiable decision-maker — a Kafka-like process where discussion accumulates and then a random exogenous shock, which changes little about what experts should believe, galvanizes the entire debate and produces a specific reaction.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Because the trigger is exogenous and expert forecasts are already roughly on track, policy timing is essentially unforecastable even when policy direction is not.
